items.headline: NSF Ocean Observatories Going Dark Off PNW Coast — Last Newport OR Station by June End; T-HUD -10.4% Enacted Path; Battery Storage Surge Nationally; Grid Modernization Lagging AI Demand; Sound Transit $34.5B Gap
items.summary: Four secondary infrastructure threads on June 7 evening. First and new: the National Science Foundation has removed all floating ocean observatories from Washington coastal waters (three stations off Grays Harbor, removed September 2025) and is removing the last remaining Oregon station (off Newport) by end of June 2026 as part of a national Trump administration dismantling of sophisticated ocean data buoy networks in the Pacific and Atlantic. For PNW operational contexts, the loss of ocean buoy data degrades: atmospheric river early detection (primary winter storm trigger mechanism), real-time ocean temperature data for fisheries and marine heat wave forecasting, wave height and storm surge data for coastal emergency management, and Pacific maritime traffic monitoring at a moment when Hormuz-disrupted shipping rerouting has elevated Pacific corridor traffic volumes. This is a structural science infrastructure degradation signal without immediate emergency implication in the current fire season context, but represents a material long-term loss for PNW integrated ocean-atmosphere monitoring. Second: T-HUD full committee markup at $92.224B (-10.4% from FY26) — the enacted-path baseline for transit capital, CDBG, and Amtrak — has not advanced to House floor scheduling as of the June 7 cycle. Sound Transit's $34.5B funding gap remains unresolved heading into the board's June capital planning session. Third: nationally, battery storage deployment is accelerating — year-to-date 2025 installations exceeded 2024's full-year 10 GW record; 2026 trajectory is tracking significantly above that pace, providing growing grid backstop function for renewable intermittency. But the 224 GW AI data center incremental load forecast through 2035 continues outpacing battery storage deployment and transmission modernization capacity. Fourth: FERC summer assessment confirms PNW drought-reduced hydropower as a specific summer grid vulnerability; SPP, PJM, and CAISO retain sufficient summer capacity for expected demand but identify wildfire-drought-heat as tail-risk scenarios.

Fourth: SCOTUS Alabama redistricting ruling (lower court reversed, expanded state redistricting latitude) remains operative in multiple states' 2026 electoral map calculations.
